MR. WAHN-INTENT OF REMARKS MADE AT PUBLIC MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. In an interview last night on the program "Encounter", the interviewer may have implied that certain remarks which I made from the floor at a public meeting in Convocation Hall of the University of Toronto last Monday suggested dishonourable motives or illegal conduct on the part of the person or persons named in the interview.
I wish to make it entirely clear that that was not my intent.
At that meeting I did defend, to the best of my ability, the decision of the government in proclaiming the War Measures Act. I reviewed in some detail the situation prevailing at the time that the decision was made, including the statements urging the government of Quebec to accede to the terrorists' demands which, if acceded to, might in my view have led to the breakdown of the civil authority of the elected government of the province of Quebec. I wish to make it entirely clear that I did not accuse or intend to accuse any individual or specific group, other than the FLQ, of dishonourable motives or illegal or dishonourable conduct. If anything I said at what was at that point a somewhat noisy meeting has given that impression, I sincerely regret it and I extend my sincere apologies to all those who may have been affected by my remarks.
Finally, I wish to make it entirely clear that I spoke at the meeting entirely on my own initiative and not at the request of any member of government, and my remarks were not based upon any private information but only upon reports which had been published in the press or referred to in this House.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Prime Minister whether, in view of the warning of APEC that the Atlantic provinces face crisis conditions of unemployment this winter, he proposes to adopt any new measures, or whether he considers APEC to be exaggerating inasmuch as he suggested yesterday we could have no assurance that Donald MacDonald was telling the truth?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO ALLEVIATE WINTER UNEMPLOYMENT CRISIS FORECAST BY ATLANTIC PROVINCES ECONOMIC COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, without agreeing with the insinuation the hon. member made about APEC not telling the truth, I might say that the government has been taking a series of measures which will have the effect of alleviating that situation. As the House remembers, in the March budget we announced that the government's cash requirements would undergo a swing of about three-quarters of a billion dollars from the previous year. This certainly is a new posture which is meant to help the unemployment situation. Last June it was announced that outlays to the provinces would increase by some $300 million to cover accelerated transfer and so on, and later it was announced that equalization payments to the provinces were to be increased by $50 million. The House knows that the student summer employment program, launched by the government, added another $73 million to current expenditures. Then, an additional $100 million was announced a month or two ago for moderate income housing. Also, in the throne speech debate the Minister of Finance announced plans for new expenditures of $60 million. All these measures, of course, add up to a serious expenditure by the government to meet these unemployment situations.
On the monetary side there has been an easing of restraints, and the money supply in private hands has increased at a seasonally adjusted annual rate averaging 12.1 per cent. I think it should be obvious to any impartial observer, Mr. Speaker, that the government is doing a great many things indeed in terms of money, money supply and fiscal measures to meet this serious unemployment situation in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, our position is that we go along with the principle of the bill, but that there are certain mechanical aspects we are concerned about. One of those pertains to review. I want to deal with this for a few moments, because this bill speaks of the same kinds of regulations as were brought in under the War Measures Act. May I point out how the War Measures Act regulations were enforced during the last war. I have before me the Defence of Canada Regulations which were in force between 1939 and 1942. You will find that even in the time of emergency, when the War Measures Act was in force, there was provision for a judicial review. I wish to read briefly from page 36 of the Defence of Canada Regulations. Subsection 26(1) reads:
Any enemy alien who has been Interned under the provisions of this Part, may within thirty days of such internment, appeal against such internment to the nearest person designated by the Minister of Justice for the purpose of hearing such appeals, hereinafter referred to as 'the Tribunal.'
That was standard procedure. I continue:
(2) A written notice of appeal signed by the appellant, shall be filed with the Tribunal by the person having the custody of such appellant, who shall transmit a copy thereof to the Registrar General of Enemy Aliens.
It is clear that a tribunal was set up, of which the trial judge was the chairman. Since the tribunal was overburdened with work, it was empowered to set up subboards headed by county court judges. What took place at that time? The special judicial board was set up and it had so many hundreds of cases to review that it was necessary to set up subboards presided over by county court judges. According to information that I finally obtained after checking with the Public Archives History Section, the Department of Justice, and with a friend of mine who formerly was a distinguished member of the RCMP but who is now retired, there were approximately between 1,800 and 1,900 detainees who applied for release; and more than 95 per cent of these were released after their applications were heard.
What I am saying is this: this bill would preserve some of the law contained in the War Measures Act regulations. It is to provide for temporary emergency powers for the preservation of public order. But there may be abuses, as I have said previously, as other members have said, and as my leader has said. Once the law is passed it will not be the Minister of Justice who will administer it;

it will not be the attorneys general of the various provinces. There will be 10,000 policemen who will interpret this law as they see fit. Under those circumstances, there are bound to be abuses.

Our amendments would seek to deal with these and other problems to which I shall refer. If a proper review board could be set up, there could be safeguards. We have already seen that about 438 people have been arrested; a great many have been released. Now, a few are being charged. Those few who are being charged, after having been detained incommunicado for a long period of time without the right to counsel, are being charged with crimes under the Criminal Code. I say that is proof that what is really wrong is that this government would not act for two years; nor would the Liberal government of the province of Quebec take its responsibilities. If these governments had shouldered their full responsibilities, these extraordinary remedies being asked for today might not have been necessary. It would not be necessary for the government to implement these extraordinary powers at this time.
So, I say that the first function is to set up a review board. That is what we suggest. We are, therefore, proposing that Bill C-181 be amended by inserting therein, next after clause 14, on page 9 thereof, the following:
15. (1) The Governor-in-Council, as soon as possible alter the coming into force of this Act, shall appoint a person holding judicial office under Her Majesty in right of Canada, who shall be called the 'Administrator', and who shall inquire into and report to Parliament from time to time upon the administration of this Act and of the Public Order Regulations, 1970.
What we are suggesting is that a superior court judge in the province of Quebec be appointed as an administrator to administer these reviews. If he were to find that the board can not handle the number of cases coming before it, he could set up subboards, as was done during the war, so that people charged would be able to have their reviews heard. Then, if there were abuses under the act-we have already heard about abuses, and I will not name names because they have already been mentioned in the debate-those abuses could be corrected by way of application to these boards. Under the bill, even if people are charged they can be held for 90 days.
We also propose:
(2)	The Administrator shall have the powers of a commissioner appointed under the Inquiries Act and shall continue as Administrator for such period after the expiration of this Act, whether by effluxion of time or by proclamation, as the case may be, as is necessary for the carrying out of his duties under this Act.
Subclause (3) would be as follows:
(3)	The Administrator shall have power to review and confirm, vary or revoke a certificate filed by an Attorney General of a province under subsection (1) of section 7 or an order made by an Attorney General under subsection (2) of section 9, and to make an order for fixing a date for trial.
Surely, whatever regulations our jurisprudence may deal with, there will be abuses. There must be abuses. Already we know from those people who have been released that mistakes have been made. Perhaps many more mistakes have been made than we are aware of because people who have been detained for a long time may be afraid to speak out now in view of the powers the government has at present. Therefore, we say that in an application before the board a date for trial should be fixed, so that justice may be done. That, to me, is the essence of a just society. What I have read constitutes our main amendment in that regard.

I take the position that generally, with one exception, this bill does not create any new crimes. It is true that membership of the FLQ is outlawed and that the procedure in our courts is reversed in the measure before us, but I still maintain that the criminal law of Canada contains all the power the government needed. All the government had to do was to stop playing politics and be pragmatists for right rather than pragmatists for opportunism, and administer the law, because they already possessed sufficient power under the Criminal Code.
What are some of these powers? Well, there is power to deal with criminal conspiracy. Criminal conspiracy means entering into an unlawful agreement for an unlawful purpose, or even a lawful agreement for an unlawful purpose. The bill before us spells out that the FLQ is an unlawful association. The clause reads:
The group of persons or association known as Le Front de Liberation du Quebec and any successor group or successor association of the said Le Front de Liberation du Quebec, or any group of persons or association that advocates the use of force or the commission of crime as a means of or as an aid in accomplishing the same or substantially the same governmental change within Canada as that advocated by the said

Le Front de Liberation du Quebec, is declared to be an unlawful association.
Mr. Chairman, that association, basically, whatever its motivation and purpose, is already within the scope of the Criminal Code. The persons who recommended, permitted or defended violence of any kind or, who, in fact, committed violence, could have been charged with criminal conspiracy. Then, there is the crime of sedition. We find, now, that people are being charged with sedition. When a crowd gets out of hand, provision is made for the use of the riot act from which certain consequences follows. Criminal conspiracy, sedition, counselling to commit an offence-all these offences are covered by the Code.
Let me get down to describing what the new bill really does. Apart from making certain that the FLQ is an unlawful association, it gives added powers to the police. I am not being critical of that at the moment, nor do I believe members of other opposition parties are critical in this regard, bearing in mind the emergency which prevails. It gives the police power to detain people without bringing charges, to interrogate them, to hold them incommunicado, to hold them without counsel. What is the purpose behind this? Normally, when a person is arrested, a charge is laid. Many times, before an accused gets the advice of counsel, he makes a statement to the police. He is generally warned, but a warning is really not one of the ingredients which go to determining whether or not such a statement is admissible at trial, subject to certain other rules which I shall not attempt to discuss at the moment. But the arrested person is generally warned and often he makes a statement. If, in the course of that statement, he incriminates himself and the court agrees that the statement was made voluntarily, the statement is admissible as evidence before a judge without jury or a judge with a jury.
Under the terms of this bill no charge need be laid immediately. The normal rights of an accused person are set aside. What really happens when a person, particularly someone who has never been in detention before, is held incommunicado for a number of days? The police have really got him in a sweat box. Along comes a police officer who asks: What information have you to give? If a person does not know when he is likely to get out of goal and there is no limitation on the time during which he can be held, what happens? He starts to tell stories.
I am not being critical in this regard, but that is the real power which this bill confers. Safeguards must be set up. We know that many people have been detained already under the War Measures Act which the bill now before us is to replace, interrogated and then released; their families did not know where they were. An independent body should be set up to minimize the possibility of this extraordinary measure being misused, bearing in mind the unusual powers which it entrusts to the police force. What the bill really means is that any door in Canada can be kicked open by the police and a man can be taken from his family, or, for that matter, the whole family can be taken away. This is why a review board is needed. This is why amendments to the mech-
November 6, 1970

anism of this bill are so necessary. But, I repeat, we went along with the bill in principle.
Now, I turn to a theme which has been mentioned by every member of my party who has spoken; it has been dealt with by spokesmen for the New Democratic Party and by spokesmen for the Creditistes, also. You cannot prevent revolution by a bill of this kind or by the War Measures Act. If I might be personal for a moment, I want to tell two stories. Every two or three years they sent Lenin and Stalin in chains to Siberia because they were disturbing the peace, advocating violence and so on. Then, under that particular government of the day they were released, but in another two years back to Siberia they went in chains.

Yes, I do, but I do not want to get off the track. I want to tell another story. I am sure my hon. friends in the New Democratic Party will appreciate this story because it is in their favour. Hon. members opposite may think this is funny, but it is not funny at all, because the same thing is now taking place in Quebec. In 1930, the bottom fell out of everything in western Canada. There were farmers in Saskatchewan who received 16 cents in total, after deduction of freight, for
1,000	pounds of beef shipped from Rosetown to Winnipeg. The price of wheat dropped to 19 cents a bushel. Machinery on the farms was repossessed. I went through that experience.
Then one day Mr. Coldwell, former leader of the C.C.F., spoke at a place called Valley Centre which has a population of around 100. About 5,000 people turned out to hear him, and I was there as a young boy, along with my father. He made a great speech. I had always thought that Mr. Coldwell was a near conservative socialist, but when it came to dealing with grievances at that time he spoke with that kind of responsibility that we would expect the leader of any party to speak with, whether or not we agreed with what he said.
His words excited, and even incited to violence, because either at a nomination meeting or shortly thereafter when he was running for my home town constituency of Rosetown-Biggar, a murder was committed. This murder was committed in the heat of a political argument by a man who was respected by the community. He was found guilty of manslaughter and served time. However, this did not change people's feelings. There was a Liberal government in the province of Saskatchewan at that time, what we called the Gardiner machine. We now have the Trudeau machine. In 1944 the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, to his credit, turned out the Gardiner machine and became premier of the province of Saskatchewan.

The point I want to drive home is this, that until government improves the social and economic conditions of the people of the province of Quebec and other provinces in Canada, the revolution will go on. All the acts and the powers of the law will not stop that revolution. Nor will they stop change. Nor will they quiet people who suffer grievances. Having been raised in this sort of sad environment, I could use some very intemperate language today, particularly with regard to the powers contained in the bill. However, I am not unsympathetic to the fact that the government, and the Minister of Justice in particular because of the position he holds, realized that there was a crisis in the province of Quebec.
The strange thing is that outside of one case I have read about-though the government may have additional information that we should have in this regard-there have been no FLQ members charged under the act; the others have been charged under the Code. I should like to know what the Minister of Justice, the Solicitor General, who is filled with words, and the Prime Minister have been doing for the last two years when they had evidence before them. The answer is that they were procrastinating. They were doing nothing. They started the fire, and now having put wood on the fire they cannot put the fire out. This is why we are standing in our places today debating extraordinary measures.
May I end with this. Revolution will not end with this bill. There has been talk about millionaires, though I am not going to get personal here. I would say to the cabinet that some were born in riches, some had a rich education and some have lived a rich life. I make a special plea to the Minister of Justice to consider seriously some of our amendments. Because if the government fails us now, it fails not only the province of Quebec and the people of Canada, but also the role of the opposition.
Somebody has said that we are the conscience of the government. At times like this, it is our job to take what may even be unpopular positions. For example, what the hon. member for Egmont did was unpopular, but I am sure one thing he did not lack was courage to vote as he did, whether his judgment will be proven to be right or wrong. This is why I ask the minister to give us a chance to suggest to him and his officers amendments to the bill. Particularly, give people the right to a review. Do not suppress or silence them. Do not hold people without giving them the opportunity to state their grievances.
We have all read in the morning papers what happened when people who were detained came before a court of justice. They were frustrated and vehement because they had been held incommunicado without the right of expression. Without the right of expression, you have oppression. This is why we feel a review board should be established. We want to be given the chance, intelligently and to the best of our ability, to suggest the kind of law that should be passed. We for our part will support the government and show that kind of responsibility that a government should expect from the members of this party and other parties.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take the opportunity of re-echoing the plea just made by the hon. member for extremely serious consideration on the part of the Minister of Justice and his government of the amendments that we are going to propose. I believe all members of the House are uneasy about this particular bill, but we have almost unanimously agreed that some measures are necessary to deal with the disorder created in the province of Quebec by the FLQ. Although we have acknowledged that necessity, we say that it is of the utmost importance that the steps taken to deal with disorder are not such as would unnecessarily deprive Canadian citizens of their fundamental rights and civil liberties.
The series of amendments that we have proposed is designed to remove vague and dangerous words from the bill; to remove principles that are not in accordance with the ordinary, recognized rules of justice. Our whole aim is to improve, make more workable and adequate what is done, not taking away from the effectiveness of this bill but taking away from it certain features that we think are dangerous to the liberty of Canadians. We have seven or eight amendments-not very many in number because this is not a long bill-which will be introduced by different members of my party. I will leave it to them, as they introduce these special amendments, to explain them in detail. However, it might be useful for me to make a rather brief summary of the amendments to be proposed.
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)
We propose an amendment to clause 6 of the bill which deals with the responsibility of an owner of a building or premises to permit meetings of the unlawful association. We say it is important to take out some of the vague words about assemblages of persons so that this clause will only deal with the owner who encourages meetings of the illegal organization, and so that it cannot be applied, owing to the vagueness of the wording employed, to, perhaps, a gathering together in classrooms or universities or other places which are not meetings of the association but at which perhaps someone in a theoretical way advocates some of the doctrines of the unlawful association.
The second amendment deals with the question of bail as it appears in clause 7 of the bill. As I think I mentioned yesterday, we propose that the granting of bail be handed back where it belongs, that is to the judiciary of this country. We do not think there is any need to distrust the judiciary. They will be advised by counsel representing the law enforcement officers of the province concerned. However, they will have a final right to say that they are not content with a mere general statement from the Attorney General that everybody should be held without bail. They will have the right to say: "We want to know why you are holding a person and depriving him of his liberty pending a hearing which may be postponed for a considerable period of time." We also think that subclause (2) of clause 7 should be amended, that holding a person for 90 days before letting him
appear to have a date fixed for trial is much too long. We propose that it be changed to 30 days.
The next amendment is to clause 8, and is of crucial importance. I particularly invite the attention of the Minister of Justice to this amendment. This is the clause that creates the retroactive application of the penal provisions of this bill. It is not itself a penal provision, it deals only with the evidence. However, by making the provision retroactive as to evidence so that acts permitted before the passing of this measure, acts which at that time were perfectly legal, can be taken as evidence upon which a conviction is made, is in effect to give retroactive effect to the bill. I will speak later with more detail on this, but I say that all across Canada, in the press and in the comments of informed people, there has been an urgent plea that this be not done. This retroactive legislation, which runs against the principles of the United Nations Universal Declaration of Human Rights, is offensive to those who say that a person who commits an act not defined as a crime cannot have criminal intent, and surely criminal intent is basic to criminal responsibility.

Mr. Chairman, before the committee adjourned for lunch, I was summarizing the amendments which different members of this party propose to move. I had reached the point of our last but one amendment which proposes that the Minister of Justice appoint a supervisory commission of three persons, not employees of the federal authority, of any provincial government or any police force, with the authority to interview persons arrested under this bill to assure they are treated according to the law, have had access to counsel, do not continue to be detained without adequate ground and have been given opportunity to be contacted by their families. It is proposed that the commission be given an opportunity to publish its findings as frequently as deemed necessary.
It would seem to me that the events of the last few days or weeks have clearly demonstrated the need for such a commission. It is all very well to say that the Bill of Rights gives certain rights, but unless there exists adequate machinery to see that these rights can be exercised then they may not be exercised. The appointment by the Minister of Justice of such a commission composed of people of the nature of special ombudsmen to deal with this particular situation which arises out of these emergency acts, and out of these perhaps necessary interferences with normal procedure, is a very important matter. I know the minister may possibly say that this can be done by voluntary organizations. Of course,

voluntary organizations can help, but they would not have the authority of a commission appointed under the direction of this Parliament, requiring that it perform this very necessary function. I believe the hon. member for York South proposes to introduce this amendment. I have no doubt he will have more to say about it at that time.
The last amendment we have on our list at the moment is an amendment to clause 15 of the bill. This would give the right to Parliament, through a motion by 10 of its members, to pray that the operation of this act be terminated and would provide that the motion would be heard at the first convenient opportunity. This amendment is in accordance with the provision now in the War Measures Act, and introduced by the Canadian Bill or Rights in 1960. It proposes the very same power for Parliament to discuss whether the time has come to end an emergency measure. It may never have to be exercised. Under clause 15, as it is presently drawn, the government by proclamation, and both houses of Parliament by joint resolution, can call for the ending of the application of the emergency measure.

I think it is important that Parliament itself be given the machinery to review these things. The authorities that are conferred here, affecting the rights of the subject, are matters that are particularly the concern of Parliament. I suggest this amendment would be a reassertion of the authority and responsibility of Parliament as to the duration or expiry of the emergency provisions of these measures which affect the liberties of Canadians.
I am going to conclude my remarks more or less in the same way as I spoke to the minister when opening my remarks. I believe that Parliament is very much on trial here, and that if the minister can see fit not only to consider seriously the amendments that are proposed but to indicate that he accedes to some of them, he will do a lot to vindicate the parliamentary process. I am not asking him to approve of something without merit or that, in his view, endangers some of the measures proposed in the bill. It would be ridiculous to ask him to do that. But I am asking him to lean over on the side of freedom, freedom of Canadians, when he comes to consider these proposals made by a responsible opposition. If he can do that, if he can see fit to accept some or all of the amendments proposed, he will be doing a lot not only to vindicate the processes of Parliament but to re-assure the Canadian people that Parliament is still in control of these things. It is not the fiat of government which alone must be used to deal with a crisis such as we face, but it is Parliament itself, the representatives of the people, whose voices are taken into account in this Parliament.

Mr. Chairman, clause 1 of Bill C-181 affords us an opportunity of making general remarks on the substance of the bill before proceeding to the examination of each clause.

November 6, 1970
Public Order Act, 1970
Judging by the almost unanimous vote that was given last night, I believe all hon. members are aware ot the importance of this bill that provides for measures to replace the War Measures Act.
The object of this bill is to prohibit any revolutionary activity on the part of the FLQ, especially in Quebec.
I agree with the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams), that this bill will not remove the remote or real causes of a revolutionary movement in Canada and particularly in Quebec.
Should this bill work out, and we hope it will, it could curb the activities of the revolutionaries by enabling us to punish them. But if Parliament does not, now or in the future, take the economic steps that would be necessary to remove the underlying causes of such activities, we shall not be able to check the revolutionaries in spite of Bill C-181 and of all the good will shown by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner).
Mr. Chairman, at the opening of each sitting, you say a prayer from which I quote the following words: Give us our daily bread. Now if the present Minister of Justice and the governments that have administered this country since Confederation had put those words into practice, we would not have to pass a bill to check the revolutionaries or outlaw revolutionary ideas in Canada.
Of course, the revolutionaries of today perhaps are not looking for their daily bread only. In fact, they have some economic or political goal to achieve. However, I believe that the majority of them have been putting up with economic conditions which, normally, should not exist in Canada and which we should seriously consider removing in the future.
I was amused on reading the speech delivered last night by the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier). He attacked those who have always supported the goverment with respect to this bill, as well as those who, as do the members of our party, realize that order and justice must be respected. I find it strange that he would not blame those who have political interests to safeguard, for we know that the disappearance of the FLQ people from Quebec might be prejudicial to some political parties which have promoted, up to now, if not revolution for the sake of democracy, at least theories which could lead to the establishment of a socialist and totalitarian state.

Some right-minded and honest government members do not approve the position of the Secretary of State who is responsible for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and who has been acting quite irresponsibly in the House for a number of years. This is a very important Crown corporation: it controls the thoughts and information of Canada. When we express grievances to him in the House he acts in an irresponsible manner and answers: I shall inquire. I do not know. I shall make an investigation. I shall tell the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation about it.
We realize that for many years, the CBC information policy has revolved around infiltration and revolutionary
ideas. Indeed, terrorist activities in Canada are unfortunately highlighted every day. Furthermore, great attention is given in programs to the speeches of those who create the political atmosphere of our country.
If indeed the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) intends to complete the clean up that he has undertaken, he should first of all consider the minister responsible for the CBC.
Mr. Speaker, we must create a favourable economic climate so that this bill does not have to remain in force for too long a time. We have felt, in this House, from the day when we have been made aware of the existence of revolutionary groups in Quebec, that a democratically elected Parliament could not give in to blackmail from some minorities. As far as we, Creditistes, are concerned, we have been challenging the present system for the past 30 or 35 years. In our opinion, reforms are needed and changes are necessary. We have offered some solutions and have not become impatient. We hope that through the democratic election process the present government and the Creditiste government which will succeed it will be able to change the present system without resorting to revolutionary methods. And this is the reason why we accept the bill introduced by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner), so as to safeguard the freedom of the majority.
Some might holler about the liberty of those who will be inconvenienced by the judicial process, who will be questioned and searched, who will have to spend a few days in jail, but I am convinced that the number of people so affected will be small as compared with the rest of the Canadian people who want to continue living in peace.
As a matter of fact, we cannot ask that, in the name of the freedom of the few, the legislation be insufficiently precise and severe. We must safeguard the majority. We have been elected for that purpose.
I have some recommendations to make with regard to the amendments we have submitted to the Minister of Justice. We deplore the fact, contrary to hon. members of a certain party sitting at my right, that the bill is still too lenient towards revolutionaries and anarchists.
This is why we will bring in some amendments. As for clause 4(g), we suggest that it be replaced by the following:
A person who advocates, promotes or engages in the use of force or the commission of crime as a means of or as an aid in accomplishing the same or substantially the same governmental change within Canada as that advocated by the unlawful association,
is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to life imprisonment.
Mr. Chairman, this amendment tends to replace clause 4(a) of the bill now under study.
The punishment provided in the bill is "not exceeding five years". The amendment extends also the scope of the bill.
Indeed, clause 4 (a), is thus drafted:
Is guilty of an indictable offence a person who a) is or professes to be a member of the unlawful association...

November 6, 1970

We maintain that not only "being a member of the unlawful association" is indictable under the law but also "the use of force, the commission of various crimes or the recourse to the commission of crimes".
Therefore, clause 4 would be replaced by Section 4A and Section 4B would be added. It would then read as follows:
Is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to be sentenced to death or to life imprisonment a person who uses force or violence for the purpose of kidnapping, keeping in seclusion, mutilating, torturing or injuring with the intent to bring about death, one or more persons, as a means of or as an aid in establishing the same government change within Canada as that advocated by the illegal association.
Some hon. members or the Minister of Justice might answer that the Criminal Code already provides for that. It does not! This amendment makes the people responsible for kidnapping and other crimes liable to be sentenced to death. According to the Criminal Code there is no more capital punishment, except for the murder of prison guards and other persons.
This amendment calls for the return to capital punishment for political crimes. In other words, kidnapping, torture, mutilation or murder, when committed for the purpose of bringing about in Canada a change such as was advocated by the FLQ, are crimes calling for the death penalty. Kidnapping, torture or murder committed in other circumstances are not punishable by death.
If our amendment were adopted, clause 5 would become clause (5) and clause 5(b) would read as follows:
A person who, knowing or having reasonable cause to believe that another person or other persons are guilty of an offence under Section 4(a), gives that other person any assistance with intent thereby to prevent, hinder or interfere with the apprehension, trial or punishment of that person for that offence, is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding fourteen years.
Mr. Chairman, our amendments are mainly aimed at making the law more comprehensive. In fact, we all know that a five-year term of imprisonment is often reduced to 20, 24 or 25 months. These sentences are too light in view of the crimes we have enumerated and which are not mentioned in the bill. I am alluding to the crimes committed by the FLQ in the Cross-Laporte case.
In the case of political murder, capital punishment should be applied. At the moment, such criminals are liable to life imprisonment.
The Criminal Code provides for "apital punishment in the case of the murder of a prison guard, a peace officer or a policeman. In my opinion, m the case of political murder such as that of Pierre Laporte, hon. members, and particularly the Ralliement Creditiste members, are right when they want to re-establish capital punishment, since who can say today who will be the next politician to be killed? Life imprisonment is too lenient a sentence for political murder.
When reading the revolutionaries' manifestos, including that of the FLQ, it is obvious that the first two steps towards revolution have already been made and that the
Public Order Act, 1970
third one will be the selective murder of politicians. This is the reason why I find it urgent to vote for the re-establishment of capital punishment for political murders like those we unfortunately witnessed recently and which we did not expect.
Because we were warned by the revolutionaries and the anarchists, we cannot plead ignorance and say there is no danger, that we need not restore in our statutes the death penalty for political murders.
Mr. Chairman, I know we will deal again during the debate, with each of these sections, in an effort to have our amendments accepted; to my mind, the bill is still not clear nor specific enough, and especially not severe enough in the light of past events and future threats.
Let us not be so naive as to think that the danger is past, because the police forces, the army, the R.C.M.P. have performed a formidable task in the last month or so; as to think the bill need not be more severe.
I feel the government is trying to please too much certain friends who, unfortunately, I know, were former friends of the Secretary of State and whose activities were more or less questionable in the past.
Mr. Chairman, we have writings that are not new, that were published throughout Quebec, that warned us of the events we know and those that could happen. Those people will not let go for they have pledged themselves to a revolutionary ideal and if the law is too complacent towards them, all the more problems will crop up.

The burden of proof in this bill remains on the Crown. It must prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt. Those of us who have participated in the criminal courts know very well that the presumptions put forward in clause 8 are not unusual. The unique part of this bill is this: under clause 4, a person who on October 16 was a member of the FLQ is guilty of an offence. This phenomenon is something which is completely new, and it involves the continued alienation of young people completely disillusioned with society as we have understood it, completely prepared to opt out of democratic processes which far too often fail to bring about the results which are needed but which are essential if any society is to work out government by consensus. It is in the rejection of this philosophy by increasing numbers of young people that we face such a grave threat today. Fortunately, at the present time most of the disillusioned young people have restricted their confrontations to reasonably peaceful means. This involves violence in words, confrontation in the streets and confrontation at meetings.

It gets hectic, it gets hot, but by far the greatest number have not yet adopted the view that terrorism, savagery and brutality, if exercised on various parts of the social anatomy of the country, will result in the changes they desire. So, when we come to deal with this phenomenon we have to make certain that we do not drive the young people, the disillusioned and the disaffected, those who can justly say they suffer deprivation under our social system, into the arms of those who advocate violence and who practice violence as a means of bringing about quickly the reforms that they demand.
If the history of the world teaches us anything, and this was made very clear by my hon. friend from Calgary North in his address this afternoon, it is that civilization is but a thin crust over the volcano of revolution and anarchy. To work out a proper balance, to contain that volcano, but not, in our effort to contain it, to pierce a hole through the crust and let through the forces of anarchy and violence within, is the task which faces the government. I give them my sympathy. It is not an easy problem; not one in which they are helped by precedents, because most governments in the past have not had to face it.
I sympathize with the government in the difficulties they have faced during the last few weeks, and realize how difficult are the decisions they have been called upon to make. I, personally, have not attempted to make matters more difficult for them by my conduct either here in the House or outside it, but I do suggest that in their approach to this problem there are two main tasks which need to be undertaken. The first is rapidly and firmly to stamp out violence, savagery and brutality as a means of government. But they must be careful not to do so in such a way as would drive more and more young people and others into becoming recruits for those who promote and practice savagery. Just a few weeks ago a group of the Weathermen in the United States, young white militants who are dedicated to savagery, brutality and violence in their way, as are many of the Black Panthers, were involved in a bank robbery in Boston, or were alleged to have been so involved, resulting in the brutal killing of a watchman and the theft of $90,000. Several of the young people concerned were brilliant university students who had recently been engaged in the advocacy of a greater measure of university reform. What is it that caused them to go over the brink? What caused them to change from being people who thought there were peaceful means of settling problems into becoming advocates of the sort of violence we saw in this country recently?
I am inclined to agree with what the Prime Minister and others have said. We have not seen the end of this situation. It might be suppressed now, but there will be outbursts all over the country in due course as more and more people become involved in this means of settling disputes. It is an object lesson for us in this House to ensure that the procedures available to us will permit greater opportunities to ventilate and solve in an honest, objective way, the problems facing society. I was encouraged to see the results of the elections in the United States. I think they were evidence, of the sound,

Here, faced with two alternatives, the American people rejected the extremism proposed on the right, an extremism which has to some extent been evident in proposals made in this House, and rejected also the views of those who thought there should be a freedom given to the extreme left to determine all problems by the use of violence. I think this was an example of an electorate showing more common sense than is suspected, sometimes, by the government or by members of this House generally.

I wish, now, to make one or two statements of our position in relation to this bill. In view of what the Minister of Justice has said, I will direct them to him. Our position, which has been consistent throughout, is this. On Friday, October 16, we as a group stated that we saw a number of things which were wrong in the way in which the War Measures Act was introduced as well as with the act itself. The day previously I had spoken in the House and said that there was another alternative, and during the course of debate we put forward that alternative. I had an opportunity to meet with the House Leader for the government and I am very happy to say that his views in this regard were the same as mine. He said, representing the views of the government, that there was an alternative so that we could approve the proclamation. It is that alternative that has brought us to the point we have arrived at today, namely, the opportunity to legislate.
When we are dealing with problems of this kind it is much better to expose and to ventilate the issue publicly in this House than to deal with it secretly by Order in Council. I know it has been argued on the government side that it was necessary to have the opportunity to make this great sweep at four or five o'clock in the morning and to pick up the suspects, but I do not think the facts bear this out. When we examine the record of the arrests, the releases, the charges laid and the names of the people who were charged, it is quite obvious that in most cases the people who were picked up and charged were not affected in one way by the proclamation made under the War Measures Act, and were picked up without any difficulty.
It was a well known fact both in Montreal and in this city that the government was toying with these two alternatives: first, invoking the War Measures Act and, second, introducing legislation. It was a very difficult decision to make, and I recognize that. I was not privy to the secrets of the Privy Council, and I am glad I was not. My suspicion is that the government was on the horns of a dilemma. Knowing the calibre of the members of the Privy Council, many members of the cabinet did not want to impose the War Measures Act but felt there were other means of achieving what was required. On the other hand, there were those who felt something should be done. There was a feeling among the people of the country that something had to be done; the people wanted some kind of action, some display of movement. There was also another, overpowering reason, which was that the authorities in Quebec obviously required addi-
Public Order Act, 1970
tional assistance and manpower for the purpose of pursuing their investigations in an attempt to solve the crimes, capture the kidnappers and obtain the release of the two people involved. I accept these as valid reasons for taking some action.
There is no doubt that at that time the receipt of the letter written by the 10 or 11 people in the province of Quebec tipped the scales in favour of imposing the War Measures Act. I know this has all been gone into to some extent, but as I see it the government of Quebec was in difficulty. The surge in public opinion, which might have been led by these 10 or 11 people, might have brought such pressure to bear on the government of Quebec that they would have found it difficult to resist, and might indeed have caused the collapse of that government. I do not subscribe to the absurd suggestion that there was a plot to overthrow the government; I think that is nonsense. But the government of Quebec might have been put in grave difficulty. So I think the first two reasons for taking some action are valid ones. The third reason is not valid.
I suspect that all future governments of Canada will have cause to rue the day when there was what appeared to be an intrusion into the affairs of a provincial government in this particular way. I am not saying that something did not need to be done; I am saying that the other method I suggested is the proper one. If a request had been made by the government for a debate of two or three hours, we would have met that request immediately. We were facing a crisis, one that could only be dealt with if the House met and acting hopefully, in unanimity agreed to invest the government with powers in excess of what it then had to meet the particular situation. Although I cannot speak for my hon. friends of the New Democratic Party, I should like to think that if a reasonable request had been made for some specific powers to meet the current problems, they also would have agreed to have a short debate so that these powers could have been given to the government.

Of course, it can be argued that these words are not absolutely essential but since the bill is, in my view, an exceptional piece of legislation, we must include those words which are required to avert any ambiguity. Indeed, on October 16, we placed our confidence in the province of Quebec to uphold the rights of prisoners to legal counsel. But they procastinated for two weeks. We had to wait for the provincial bar association, the federal government and the judicial body to issue statements in this regard before the government of Quebec recognized that the regulations proclaimed under the War Measures Act did not infringe upon a right enshrined in the Bill of Rights.
I believe we should take good account of this experience and include in the bill before us the words "A person who, without legitimate grounds the onus of which lies upon the said person".
To my mind, clause 5 should be amended so as to maintain the existing privilege in favour of the spouse. You will recall that the Criminal Code says: section 5 deals with complicity after the fact. The Criminal Code makes exception for the spouse who helps her husband to escape. And I do not think we have the right to cancel this provision of the Criminal Code which is centuries old.
In clause 6 there are, I believe, two different concepts. Lines up to 20 prohibit meetings of FLQ cells, and the second part prohibits meetings by other groups for a very definite purpose and not only meetings per se.
Clause 7 as it stands now I believe is unacceptable, and I would also draw the attention of the minister to a legal error in clause 7 (2) of the bill. Under the bill, and particularly under clause 7(3) as well as under the amendment introduced today, it is impossible to issue an order to a judge of the superior court of criminal jurisdiction in the province of Quebec because in our country it is absolutely unthinkable for a judge of the appeal court, Crown side, to set the date of trial-and as I was saying, it is impossible to give orders to a judge of the court of the sessions of the peace other than by mandamus or in resorting to control power.
Section 8 requires clarification and some remarks on section 9, paragraphs (2 and (3) would be in order.
In respect to sections 10 and 11, concerning search, I wish all the rights recognized in the Criminal Code to the owner of the seized belongings were safeguarded. There is even no provision for an official entry to be made of the seized items as a matter of record.
Concerning section 12, I submit that interference of politics in the judiciary seems an unfortunate way of settling the problem. I shall have other solutions to suggest.
Finally, I would suggest to the minister that the logical order of the sections following section 6 should be as follows. After section 6 should come the basic sections 10 and 11 on search, then section 9(1), concerning arrest without warrant, and afterwards, sections 9(2) and (3), concerning appearance before the court. Following that should come section 7, dealing with detention, and section
Public Order Act, 1970
7(2) regarding directions for expediting trial, and lastly, section 8, concerning the rule of evidence.
These are roughly the remarks I intend to make. Besides, I shall suggest amendments to improve the French wording of the bill.

subtopic: PUBLIC ORDER (TEMPORARY MEASURES) ACT, 1970 PROVISION OF EMERGENCY POWERS FOR PRESERVATION OF PUBLIC ORDER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the crisis we are now going through and are trying to deal with goes beyond political considerations, and I believe we should strive to find solutions without playing politics with such a serious question.
It is in that spirit, Mr. Chairman, that I would like to make a few remarks, for it is not my intention to keep the House very long.
Mr. Chairman, when the war measures were put forward by the government, this party put all its confidence in the government and we all supported the government's efforts to strike at the root of evil.
My Quebec colleagues and I had warned our party that regardless of the position it would take in this regard, we felt duty bound to vote for the War Measures Act. We did so because we believed without question what the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) had told us. We did not want to question his word and acted accordingly.
Bill C-181 is now before us. I do not wish to discuss the sections of that bill. Thank God, there are enough lawyers to do so and I do not believe I should venture in such a complex field. I shall leave it to the disciples of Themis to make the best legislation possible out of the bill now before the House.
Mr. Chairman, it is understood that this bill is imperfect. Having been conceived by human beings, the contrary would be astonishing. Still we must make every possible effort to make it more explicit so as to meet the needs which concern us at this time.
It is therefore, Mr. Chairman, in the common interest of the Canadian people and especially of the people of the province of Quebec, that the government pay special attention to the suggestions made by the members of the opposition.
I should like to insist on this: the amendments proposed by the members of the Ralliement creditiste, the New Democratic Party or the Conservative Party have but one goal-to make the act as efficient as possible.
On various occasions, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has also held the opposition responsible for applying the war measures. Time and time again he said that we had given complete support to the government and that, because of this, we had to accept our responsibilities.
If it is true, Mr. Chairman, that we have assumed some responsibility by approving the implementation of war measures, it follows that the government should go half way and show a disposition to accept amendments which, I say it again, are as generous and as well intentioned as possible.

November 6, 1970
Public Order Act, 1970
In introducing those amendments, we do not seek any political aim or capital. We are seeking only the common welfare of the population. So I would like to make a special appeal to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) so he will take into serious consideration the amendments presented to him.
Knowing what those on the government side may be thinking, it is clear that they do not have-any more than we do for that matter-the monopoly on science. Now, I think that they should give appropriate consideration to the amendment presented by my colleague from Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) as well as to those introduced by other parties.
I could yet say many things in that respect. For instance, I could say that, having heard certain speeches by certain members of the government, including the hon. members for New Westminster (Mr. Hogarth), for Sherbrooke (Mr. Gervais) and for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand), according to whom the danger of revolution was hanging over the province of Quebec, I could say that if it is true that the government knew all the aspects of the situation which existed in the province of Quebec, one can only wonder why they did not act before.
It will be said, as the hon. Minister for Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) is probably going to say, that it was necessary to wait for the province of Quebec to ask the assistance of the federal government. I wonder how long the federal government, aware of the danger and of the various aspects of this situation, would have waited before taking the necessary measures.
It is the duty of any government to see that the security of its citizens is maintained in all occasions. I would ask my hon. friends opposite to stop making such statements because, by doing so, they confirm that we are right when we urge the government to reveal to the population all available and relevant facts so that we can judge their value ourselves.
Mr. Chairman, I would conclude my remarks by asking once more the Minister of Justice to accept the amendments proposed to him since they only have one purpose: facilitating the elimination of the present crisis.

subtopic: PUBLIC ORDER (TEMPORARY MEASURES) ACT, 1970 PROVISION OF EMERGENCY POWERS FOR PRESERVATION OF PUBLIC ORDER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, like a number of other members in this House yesterday, I voted for the bill before us with a considerable degree of hesitation. The bill before us is intended to deal with a matter which is unique in the history of our country. Never before have Canadians really had to deal with terroristic politics. For the first time, in a very serious and fundamental way, we face the problem of dealing with the conflicting objectives of freedom and orderliness, that is to say, conflicting at times but conflicting certainly when there is a terroristic group in society.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
The FLQ have been active in Canada for at least eight years. They have committed murder. They have committed acts of bombing. They have caused the derailment of trains. They have committed a number of other acts highly objectionable in any civilized, democratic society. Therefore, there is no question in anyone's mind that such a group and, such politics must be dealt with in a very serious and concentrated way. This kind of activity in recent weeks culminated in two kidnappings, one murder and the intimidation of government.
During this time the federal government declared that there was an apprehended insurrection in the country. It was the judgment of at least 16 members of this House that this was not the case. It is our view that there is indeed a serious malaise in the political culture of Canada. There have, indeed, been reprehensible and serious kidnappings, but there was not an apprehended insurrection. Therefore, we voted against a measure which proclaimed that there was such an insurrection. And we found, in terms of the regulations that came with that proclamation, that there were taken away from Canadians basic liberties acquired over hundreds of years of history. We did not believe this was necessary to deal with what was admittedly a very serious situation.
I am not going to go over the whole ground as to whether or not the government was right in what it did. As I say, a number of us believed it was wrong. History will be the judge of that. But I think what we have to face today, and what this bill proposes to face, is the question: What do we do now? It is not what do we do now in terms of welfare legislation, regional development programs or providing linguistic justice, all of which remedies are indeed necessary to deal with the very seraous problems of French Canada and Quebec, but: What do we do in terms of the Criminal Code? That is really what is at issue.
What do we say is to be criminal activity? What can be done to deal with the very serious problems associated with Quebec, in terms of criminal law? In the law books of this country we have laws pertaining to sedition, conspiracy, intimidation and kidnapping. If you look at this bill with care, you will find there are no changes at all made there. The government, instead of arguing that some improvement must be made in these areas to deal with terroristic politics, has said, "Really what we need to do is, first of all, ban the FLQ." That is one central, specific part of the bill. Further, the government proposes to extend the powers of arrest, detention and search.
In the view of a number of hon. members, certainly in the view of a number of members of this party, whether or not we support this measure on third reading will be determined by the flexibility of the government and its willingness to accept reasonable amendments. It is our view that we must deal with terroristic politics and, therefore, that we must make some changes in the criminal law. But the frame of reference for us is the broad one of how we deal with criminal politics, on the one hand, and preserve freedom on the other. It is our view
[Mr. Ricard.l
November 6, 1970

that no limitation on Canadian freedom-none whatsoever-is justified beyond that which is necessary to deal with the politics of the FLQ.
Let us begin by asking what are the existing powers of arrest, detention and search. The first point that can be made is that a man in Canada can only be arrested if he has or is about to commit a criminal offence. Secondly, such a man must be taken before a justice of the peace and be charged within 24 hours. Thirdly, police in this country at present can conduct a search only with a warrant, and there must be reasonable and probable grounds for conducting such a search. What does the new legislation propose? There are a number of changes, but in my view the most important and most basic to this question are, first, an extension of the powers of arrest and detention, second, an extension of the powers of search and, third, clause 8 which is the provision of ex post facto law. These are serious changes in the fundamental rights of Canadians acquired over hundreds of years of our history, and they are not to be discussed or dismissed lightly. The question we must answer is: Should we make the changes in these three areas to deal with the FLQ?
As I mentioned earlier, one thing has been decided. In the bill we have in effect declared that the FLQ is an illegal, violent conspiracy. The bill makes its kind of politics illegal. Therefore, the other changes in basic law as they affect our Canadian rights, changes concerning arrest, detention and search, must be intended to do one of two things-on the one hand, to prevent crime by the FLQ or associated bodies or, on the other, to catch those involved in a crime that was committed in the past.
The question then is: Do we need the extension of powers in these areas to deal with this situation? I put it to the Minister of Justice, not as a rhetorical but as a genuine question: If we now assume that there is no state of insurrection, that there is no impending riot in the immediately foreseeable future, but there is a terroristic group with which we must deal in a serious way, could this not be done merely by extending the present powers of search? If we consider what is involved in the present powers of search, in my view all that is required is to extend those powers. At present, as the Minister of Justice well knows, before you can search a Canadian's home there must be a warrant and there must be reasonable and probable grounds for searching it. The bill provides for an extension of these grounds, and in my view perhaps that is all we need at this time, if the grounds could be further changed from reasonable and probable to mere suspicion.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
Let us accept the time period for this bill, until the end of April. If it were declared that during this period whole areas of Montreal, some other city, another part of the province or, indeed, any other part of Canada needed to be systematically searched, this could be done under the proposal I make of extending the powers of search and
Public Order Act, 1970
no warrant would be needed. Then when a search was made, instead of arresting people and bringing them in without laying charges and keeping them in jail for long periods of time, no such arrest could be made unless there were evidence of past criminal activity or intended criminal activity. In other words, the existing provision of the Criminal Code would have to be used. If we are really interested in preserving freedom in Canada, particularly in Quebec because that is where this activity is located, this is the kind of provision-the first step, if you like; the first, minimal erosion of our freedoms- that we should be considering. It is up to the government to prove that something else is required.
I assert that there is no insurrection now, and the government has acknowledged that by the title of this bill for the preservation of public order. If it has reasonable grounds for believing that before the end of April a riot is going to take place, a kidnapping or any other kind of criminal activity by the FLQ, a successor body or a body sympathetic to the FLQ, it could move through these extended powers of search. What would be the advantages of taking this much more limited approach, Mr. Chairman? Obviously, the first is that the existing freedoms would remain unchanged, with the exception of the power of search. Secondly, a well equipped, dedicated and hardworking police force, in my view, would be able to deal quickly with FLQ actions or intended actions. Finally, and this is really an elaboration of the first point, such limited kind of change in our law would enable us to maintain a basically free society and yet deal with the kind of malaise that we all wish to exorcise.
I would like the Minister of Justice to depart from the kind of partisan politics in which he indulged the other day and address himself, at some point in the debate, to the very serious question as to whether or not there is a need to extend governmental power beyond that which I am proposing.

So, Mr. Chairman, I justify our action in that sense. We have to take critical action to meet a critical situation, one on which the public conscience demanded action. I shall never look back at myself in that respect and wonder why I voted as I did, and as I will no doubt vote in the next few days. Nonetheless, in what I say this afternoon I shall pose the question of whether the government could have taken a better course than the one it has followed. A better course would have been to follow the sensible suggestions that have been made, not only in recent weeks but for some time. Had the government taken that action, I suggest we would not now be engaged in this debate.

November 6, 1970
Public Order Act, 1970
May I present a sort of philosophical postscript to all this, Mr. Chairman, before I get into the meat and potatoes of my argument. I look at the people involved, the inner-circle of the government, the people before the courts in Quebec, the people being hunted, the people whose names are in the news at the very heart of today's tragic drama in Canada, and it reminds me of Victor Hugo's "Les Miserables". In that novel, all the great characters came together in the last few chapters, arrayed on one side or other of barricades erected in the streets of Paris. Some were on one side of the barricade when they could have been expected to be on the other. Such is the kaleidoscopic way of change in which lives are moulded in our times.
Much has been made of the way in which this legislation was initiated. I think the answer is clearly to be found in statements made by the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition early in this story, on October 16. The Prime Minister's position would not have led to legislation being considered here today because, as he said then as reported at page 194 of Hansard:
Following the passage of enough time to give the government the necessary experience to assess the type of statute which may be required in these circumstances, it is my firm intention to discuss with the leaders of the opposition parties the desirability of introducing legislation of a less comprehensive nature.
But there the Prime Minister is referring to what has still to be produced, the long-term measure. I think that is a fair reading of everything the right hon. gentleman had to say on that page. A few minutes later, the Leader of the Official Opposition said, as reported at page 196 of Hansard:
Nevertheless, I urge that the government instead of seeking the approval of the House for the measure it has already taken, the invoking of the War Measures Act, should heed what is said in the House today and should at the earliest possible date bring in a bill with much more restricted powers, many more safeguards with regard to review, and of a much more limited duration.
Mr. Chairman, that is the legislation we are considering today. When we talk about the conscience of Parliament, this shows that the leadership has indeed come from Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition. It seems strange that we should be discussing a situation in which so far approximately nine out of every ten people arrested should not have been. In normal times, those of us familiar with the background of English common law would quote the old saying that it is better that ten guilty men should go free than that one innocent man should be punished. That is the philosophy that guides us in more sober and less dramatic times.
There are those of us on this side of the House particularly, and I imagine there are those on the other side of the House too, who are concerned that there is such a large number of arrests. Under the arbitrary provisions of the War Measures Act, people can suddenly be arrested and deprived of their liberty in the middle of the night. After several days they may be released. This is an abuse, and it is to prevent abuses that we on the opposition are suggesting certain amendments to the Minister 
of Justice. We shall be fighting for the adoption of these amendments next week when we resume consideration of this bill.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
I join in the eloquent pleas made by others to the Minister of Justice. He should pay due regard to what we are trying to do. We are not trying to discombobulate him. We are not trying to embarrass him in any way. We are trying to satisfy the feelings of Canadians and make sure that, as far as possible, criminal elements shall be dealt with in a just way. There are many in this House who fought against the horror that our planet experienced only three decades ago, a horror in which the jackboot rang on cobblestoned streets in the middle of the night and in which people disappeared, some never to reappear. Some went to the gas ovens; others reappeared as impoverished refugees if they were lucky enough to escape.
We ask: Why cannot that happen here if we have arbitrary action on such a scale and when so many errors have been committed? One can only assume that our government, which is supposed to be civilized and to represent our civilization, harboured no effective forethought for dealing with this emergency. All this while these Maoists, Marxists and other extreme leftists in the province of Quebec have been preaching their doctrines. They are economic doctrines, but these people are smart enough to use the political wagon of separatism in furthering their idea. They have been around for some time.
Last night on television the Prime Minister used two words. I will not mention them now; I will merely ask: To whom do those two words the Prime Minister uttered apply? For years the members of the Conservative party have asked for a royal commission to look into the causes of crime in Canada. Our large cities, and Montreal in particular-the city which is bearing the brunt of these awful times-have been faced with the problem of the Mafia. Latterly, Montreal has been faced with the problem of terrorism. The combination of the Mafia and terrorism has been more than the police force of that city could handle without outside help. That outside help has now been provided.
This situation is not new. For seven years we have asked for this royal commission. The present Prime Minister, as well as preceding prime ministers, when asked about this matter just shrugged it off. No action was taken. How would you describe a person who makes that sort of decision? One year ago Mr. Saulnier of the city of Montreal, who knew of the terrible problem that city's police forces were facing, who knew that those men were literally being driven beyond endurance in their fight against terrorism and the war against the Mafia, requested of the government a royal commission to look into certain matters pertaining to his city. That very sensible request on the part of the most important public servant to serve outside the federal and public services of Canada was not acceded to. What was the response to that request? It was a shrug. I ask: How would one characterize a person who makes that sort of response?
November 6, 1970

Let us consider the statement made in this House on the day before it was decided to send forces into Montreal early on the morning. How would one characterize a person who makes such statements? What sort of adjectives could one apply to that sort of person? What would one call a man who proclaims himself as an apostle of instant action, yet does nothing? Good God, Mr. Chairman, this government has waited for years and years before acting; the crisis piles up and now it asks us to give our approbation and blessing for what it has done. The government will gain approval, because steps must be taken. But we will not trust the government to administer these measures efficiently, because innocent people may be dragged in. After all, that is why we are fighting as best we can, to bring safeguards into the legislation that is before the House.
Sir, I meant to leave to the end of my remarks the adjectives that the Prime Minister of this country used when speaking on television last night. He tried to suggest that the words would apply to what others would do in this situation and that they do not apply to himself. Considering the way in which he dealt with the request for the appointment of a royal commission, and the way he acted in certain matters a couple of years ago, the adjective that should apply to him, that he said should apply to others, is "wishy-washy".
