EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: UNITED NATIONS-MORE EFFECTIVE ROLE IN PREVENTING MILITARY AGGRESSION, ETC.
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should take initiatives for United Nations reform to make that institution a more effective instrument for the prevention of military aggression, for the settlement of international disputes, and to promote co-operation, peace and prosperity in particular, to:
1. provide that the decisions of the Security Council be enforceable;
2. provide that the unused provisions of the charter be activated;
3.	provide that the International Court of Justice be empowered to interpret the United Nations charter;
4.	provide for universality of membership;
5.	provide for the establishment of global authorities related to the United Nations to deal with serious global problems
U.N.-Prevention of Military Aggression such as the environment, population, development of seabed resources, and economic and social stability;
6.	provide for a United Nations stand-by peace force.
He said: Mr. Speaker, on October 24 this year the peoples of the world commemorated the twenty-fifth anniversary of the ratification of the United Nations charter. On that occasion many of us suggested that we should not at that time merely celebrate that anniversary in the sense of commemorating the setting-up of the United Nations but, rather, that we should take steps to reform the United Nations, to correct its failings and to make it a much more effective organization.
During the previous session I had the honour to sponsor a private member's motion in this House asking for the reform of the United Nations charter. That motion was debated in the House on February 9, 1970. Since the debate on that motion several speeches have been made which have given me great encouragement. One of the those was made in New York by U Thant, Secretary General of the United Nations. The second speech was also made by U Thant, here in Ottawa during August when he was addressing the Conference of World Federalists. As a result of various remarks and the speeches of the Secretary General of the United Nations, I have brought forward the motion we are discussing. It sets out six points. These six points are the same as those put forward by the Secretary General of the United Nations.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
When I put forward my resolution last year, many people participated in the debate. They said that my proposals were unrealistic and unacceptable. The six points which I am now putting forward are the same as those put forward by the Secretary General, a man who has served the United Nations since its inception, and as Secretary General for many years. He put forward these proposals because he thinks the United Nations needs reform and that these proposals will help bring it into the seventies to do the job it must do.
These six proposals are as follows: First, the decisions of the Security Council must be enforceable; second, the unused provisions of the charter should be activated; third, the International Court of Justice must be empowered to interpret the United Nations charter; fourth, steps should be taken toward universality of membership; fifth, there should be established under the United Nations, global authorities to deal with serious world problems such as environment, population control, development of the seabed resources, and economic and social stability; sixth, the United Nations should have a standby peace force.
I refer to some of the remarks made by the Secretary General in a speech in Ottawa. He said as follows:
In a very important sense, the United Nations is in a transitional stage. Effective and sensible world approaches to world problems are urgently required. The United Nations, for the reasons mentioned, has not yet been charged with that full responsibility of adequate authority to discharge it. But the United Nations has to be the active and vital process within which world policies are made or changed, within which agreement and consensus must be reached on major issues among member states, and where agreed decisions must be carried out

November 6, 1970
U.N.-Prevention of Military Aggression
on behalf of the world community. That process is only embryonic, in comparison with the needs, but we know that it *nust be fully developed . . .
I recently said that strengthening the United Nations should be not just a desire but an obsession ... X would like to summarize very briefly the immediate steps I see as indispensable.
He then deals with the six points which read as follows:
First and foremost, the decisions of the United Nations, particularly of the Security Council, must be enforceable.
Second, unused provisions of the charter, which can add greatly to international peace and security, should be activated.
He then refers to subsidiary bodies for fact-finding and conciliation, as follows:
Third, the International Court of Justice must be empowered to interpret the United Nations charter. Our goal should be the acceptance by all member states without exception of the compulsory jurisdiction of the International Court of Justice in all international legal disputes.
Fourth, I have mentioned earlier that I consider the idea of the universality of the United Nations the priority item of this year's agenda for world affairs.
Since U Thant delivered that speech, Canada has established diplomatic relations with China. This matter will soon come before the United Nations for a vote to determine whether the People's Republic of China should be admitted to the seat now held by Taiwan. If we are to properly act upon the request of the Secretary General which would make the United Nations a universal body, Canada should support this admission to the United Nations on a full basis. This is what our government said they would do, but we do not yet know in which way they will support it or whether they will vote in favour of the matter being a serious question.
The fifth proposal the Secretary General made to the delegates in Ottawa is as follows:
Fifth, I have urgently recommended that global authorities related to the United Nations be established to deal with serious global problems.
He then dealt with the threat to our environment and the need for an international agency to deal with world pollution and conservation problems. He said:
It is my sincere hope that the United Nations Conference on the Human Environment, which is to meet in Stockholm in 1972 on the invitation of the government of Sweden, will take the first steps toward the establishment of such an agency.
As hon. members know, the Deputy Secretary General, who will head the world conference on environmental problems, is a Canadian, Mr. Maurice Strong. He is the former head of the Canadian International Development Agency. We wish him luck in his new task. I hope the Canadian government will fully support him and the conference in the work to be done.
The Secretary General, referring to resources of the seabed, said:
-I hope that steps will swiftly be taken to establish the proposed international regime to administer the resources of the seabed, generally recognized as "the common heritage of mankind".
Sixth, the United Nations urgently needs a standby force a recommendation I made to the General Assembly some years ago. Progress in the Committee of 35 may be encouraging, but 
we have a long way to go before such a force becomes an actuality. In my view, a ready, trained, standby force is a prerequisite for effective maintenance of international peace and security.
These are the six points that U Thant feels are necessary to reform the United Nations in its twenty-fifth anniversary year. Why is change needed? As I attempted to point out last year, the United Nations was formed following World War II. There was great hope that it would be the proper institution to handle problems of international conflict and to deal with the terrible problems of war such as confronted the world from 1939 to 1945. Unfortunately, that has not been the case. Although there have been no world wars since World War II, there have been 48 major and minor wars. There has hardly been an occasion since 1945 when there has not been some type of war going on somewhere in the world. Even though they have not been atomic wars, the people who die as a result of them are dying just as cruelly and with as much terror as in a war on a world scale. The only difference is that in a world war, more people die.
We should take preventive measures before there is another world war. We should not wait until we are involved in another world conflict before thinking seriously about these matters. The present situation is almost one of world anarchy. In the past week we have been discussing the need for systems of order in this country and laws to deal with terror and criminals. We see this need within our national boundaries but we have not reached the point where we have effective institutions to deal with anarchy, terror and war between nations or on a world level.
The United Nations must be elevated to a higher level so that it can properly negotiate settlements with effectiveness when world disputes arise. One of the greatest threats to world peace at the present time is the situation in the Middle East. There have been temporary ceasefires, but unless we deal with the cause of that war it could be the spark that would once again develop into a world conflict. As I say, we should not wait until these things take place but we should act now, while we have time, to strengthen our world institutions, our world court and our United Nations so these things cannot happen.
o (4:10 p.m.)
I do not suggest that the United Nations has been a failure over the last 25 years. I think that if the United Nations had not been in existence, the world would be in a much worse state. The United Nations, even as it stands, is valuable, but it is not yet adequate. However, because I do not want to leave the impression that the United Nations has failed in all areas, I would point out that it has been a very real success especially with respect to the specialized agencies, the World Health Organization, the Food and Agriculture Organization and ECOSOC with respect to economic and social questions.
It has also been a very real success in the area of decolonization. Many countries in Asia and Africa have been released from colonial status and have been set up as fully independent states which are today members of
November 6, 1970

the United Nations. Great progress has been made in this field since 1945. There have also been successes in connection with peacekeeping, especially in Kashmir, Cyprus and the Congo and, for ten years, in the Middle East. I would hope that these minor successes in some areas would bring home to us the great successes we could achieve if we improved and reformed the United Nations so that in other areas it could act more effectively and with teeth.
It is for this reason I have brought this motion before the House in the twenty-fifth anniversary year of the organization, in the hope that the House will approve it. This is not a private member's bill; it is merely a resolution which I am putting to the House. It would be a set of goals to which hon. members could subscribe, goals which we in this country should try to reach. I understand that not all of these six items can be put into effect immediately if we approve this resolution. Even if all the nations of the world approve these points, these things could not be done this year. But if we start by accepting and approving these goals, it means the first step has been taken. We have to set goals for ourselves so that we can work out means of achieving them.
I earnestly ask the House and the government to accept these goals. A year ago when I made a suggestion like this, people thought it was too idealistic, but now these things are being said by the Secretary General of the United Nations and by many other people in the world. I hope we can go forward and make the twenty-fifth anniversary year of the United Nations a year when we do not merely raise flags and say a few nice words in favour of the United Nations, but one in which we look at the past, examine the shortcomings of the institution and take steps to correct them.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: UNITED NATIONS-MORE EFFECTIVE ROLE IN PREVENTING MILITARY AGGRESSION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the trouble with the hon. member's resolution is that it covers such a wide field that it is difficult in the hour in which we are permitted to discuss world affairs, rather than domestic affairs, to give precise consideration to any one of the six items he mentions. I say this not in any way to be critical but merely as a warning that the remarks I intend to make may not be as incisive as they should be.
James Reston, surely one of the most thoughtful commentators of our age, in an August birthday message to the United Nations which appeared in the New York Times of August 12, said the soldiers had been dominating world events for the past few years but that the diplomats were now stirring again. The diplomats have always been in the awkward position of seeking to anticipate the future, and they are now beginning to think they can at least talk about the world beyond the present wars.
Whenever I become discouraged at the futility of some of the debates which go on in the General Assembly, I console myself by thinking that at least some of the issues are being discussed and that discussion is better than violence. I propose to discuss briefly two or three of the issues in this speech in support of the hon. member's resolution. One of the issues that I think the hon.
U.N.-Prevention of Military Aggression member is right in asking us to reflect upon concerns the essential need for universality of membership in the United Nations. Usually, when discussions on this subject take place we think, quite understandably I suppose, of the substitution of the government of the People's Republic of China for the Nationalist Government of China. I, with others, believe that this is inevitable and that the sooner it takes place, the better. But there are other parts of the world which remain outside membership.
I do not intend to go into the merits, but if we are frank about this question of universality, we have to consider a formula to provide for the "split" countries, the Koreas, the Viet Nams, north and south, and the two Germanys. I also believe, though I have got into trouble at times for saying so, that there are many people, particular in Africa, particularly in countries like Rhodesia and the Republic of South Africa, Angola and Mozambique who, because of the authoritarian nature of the regimes under which they are forced to exist and the obscenity of apartheid and other measures which frustrate, to use a somewhat eloquent phrase, the flowering of their citizenship, are not in any meaningful sense represented at the United Nations. So when we talk of universality, let us be very clear that there are still a large number of people in the world who have not yet been able to enjoy the membership we seek for them.
The peace force proposal can be discussed briefly. I hope hon. members will agree, modestly. The idea of a peace force is not a new one but its usefulness has been underlined, I am sure, by the report of the subcommittee of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence which reported some months ago. I trust the report was the subject of urgent consideration by the government on this very point. In other words, we have a somewhat up-to-date and, if I may say so, thoughtful, well documented report of a subcommittee of a Standing Committee of the House of Commons which provides all the information and forward thrust that I think we will get at this stage for the usefulness of a peace force.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
The last point I want to make, since I am sure other hon. members will want to indicate their support for this resolution, relates to the large item that is covered in paragraph 5 of the resolution before the House. I refer to United Nations authority to deal with serious global problems such as the environment, population, development of seabed resources, and economic and social stability. I think so much is encompassed in this paragraph that it rather diffuses the proper emphasis that must be placed on one or two other items.
Surely the world has had all the warning it needs by now of the serious danger that man is doing to his environment and the very precious balance that it is our obligation to keep. In some parts of the world we know that this balance has been drastically upset. Indeed, in some areas there is doubt whether there is in fact remedial action that can be taken to save the dead seas,

November 6, 1970
U.N.-Prevention of Military Aggression not of biblical times but of the present day. Having said that, I welcome the proposal in regard to the Stockholm conference on pollution. My only reservation is that it takes mankind so long to get around to organizing these conferences; and this one will not meet, I think, until 1972.
The second item in paragraph 5 has to do with population. I think here we must be realistic too. While it should never be part of the policy of the government of Canada to impose birth control methods on peoples of other cultures and other countries, nevertheless we should not resist making available, hopefully under UN auspices, both funds and technology to meet the situation so that we will not be faced with another encroachment upon the quality of life, as it were-a world where there are in fact too many people. I do not suppose that I will be around in the year 2000, but I am satisfied that I do not want to be if the world does contain the 7 billion people that present population projections indicate.
When people talk of the great open spaces of the world and say that all we have to do is to fill these spaces with people, they cease to get to the central issue. If the people of the earth are put into these now empty spaces, what type of lives will they live? I think there are techniques that man in his wisdom has evolved to find answers to what could be a very terrible disaster. I hope there will be set up, I do not like the word "commissioner" but certainly somebody in the United Nations responsible for dealing with the problems that man faces because of a rapidly escalating population.
The last issue I want to speak about very briefly is the technology man now possesses to exploit the last unexploited part of the earth, the seabed. Here I hope man does not fall into the trap that he fell into during the great escapades of exploitation in the last few centuries which have culminated, I think, in the quite irresponsible exploitation of the last 100 years. This is an area where man, if he is to exploit, must exploit together. Man has to exploit, remembering that these resources do not belong to any one country but belong, surely, to all men. He has to remember that because this country, for example, has been blessed, through an accident of geography, with a large coastline-I believe the largest coastline in the world-there are other people in landlocked areas and in undeveloped parts of the world who, surely, have rights equal to those which belong to all men-those resources which are on the ocean floor, the seabed and below the seabed.
Therefore, I think it is essential that some regime be set up to deal with the techniques, with all of the "terrible engines", if I may call them that, of exploitation which could be unleashed unless all man's wisdom and generosity is used to harness them for the benefit of all men. Without this regime we shall be in for serious trouble.
I am sure all hon. members are delighted to note that some forward steps have been taken. It is peculiar that when technology demands that man find a solution that
[Mr. Fairweather.l
is apart from ideology, man is often able to do this. I for one think that the curse of this and other ages has been the ideological dogmas that influence men to take certain positions. When man can separate himself from ideology and deal with what I might call the real problems, he usually succeeds in finding an accommodation.
I cite just one or two examples of this. I am advised that one of the most useful initiatives that has been taken in this regard is the North Pacific convention on halibut. The four or five countries of various political stripes that harvest the seas have something in common: they need to be assured of a constant supply of resources from the sea. This is why such a convention is essential to them. It does not really matter whether a man is a citizen of the U.S.S.R., Japan, Canada or the United States, or whether he is a Liberal, Progressive Conservative, Republican or what have you; the resources of the sea must be conserved. This is the impetus that has made such a convention possible.
I think this sort of action to protect the seabed is essential, and I must say I look forward to debates in the UN to evolve regimes for exploitation purposes-or for harvesting, if that is a better word-for the benefit of everybody on this earth. This matter is urgent because if man exploits without regulation, he will pollute. It is urgent because it is essential to co-ordinate research and to supervise the exploitation. It is urgent because unless we have a regime under international auspices, surely we will have only licensed entrepreneurs who have only national ambitions-and this I think would be tragic. I warned the House that the very general nature and the very wide number of issues covered by the resolution that we are discussing today means that members do not have the opportunity that they might perhaps like to have to hone and sharpen their comments. Therefore, I am making this apology for being somewhat general.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson said-I am paraphrasing his words-that the United Nations was in danger of sinking on a point of order. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp), in his speech to the UN General Assembly last year, warned the UN about the proliferation of reports and of paper. I think that we, too, might take warning from these words. I hope that a committee of United Nations will deal very seriously with the problems raised by the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
I think it is a very happy fact that this year the distinguished President of the United Nations is a very wise and knowledgeable gentleman, Mr. Eric Hambro, who does not put up with some of the niceties of the lateness and proliferation of committees' reports and, if I may say so, of the nonsense encountered in diplomatic forms that unhappily have scarred an otherwise rather good record of the UN.
The last thing I wish to say on this subject is that when some of us think of the 25 years of the UN and are
November 6, 1970

frustrated about its thrust and its eifectiveness, we should remember, as the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) reminded us, of the tremendous work of the specialized agencies. If there had been no UN, it is doubtful that the World Health Organization, the Food and Agricultural Organization, UNESCO, the specialized agencies dealing with international development, and so on, could ever have reached their present degree of helpfulness to man.
Therefore, when we get upset about sterile debates-as we often do when we listen, for instance, to the old debate on China coming up again-we should take encouragement from the specialized agencies and their work and remember, as the hon. member said, what might have happened if the UN itself had not been established 25 years ago. Someone reminded us that our world is too small for anything but truth and too dangerous for anything but brotherhood. I suggest that this is the birthday greeting that should be very much part of our thoughts when we think of the 25 years of the United Nations.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: UNITED NATIONS-MORE EFFECTIVE ROLE IN PREVENTING MILITARY AGGRESSION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I share the difficulty of the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) in that I, too, find the subject so broad as to encompass the whole future history of mankind. It is a motion that rather lends itself to generalities. Nevertheless, I too want to say that the motion before us is both forward-looking and, in my view, realistic and it has our enthusiastic support.
I think it was the late President Kennedy who said that in the nuclear world, peace is the rational end of rational man. It sometimes seems to me that it should be our first preoccupation, although it is often our last. In the type of age in which we live, survival depends upon an orderly world, an orderly world in turn depends upon some system of world law or order and this depends upon the evolution of a world community. It is trite to say that technology has made the world into a neighbourhood, but it is a neighbourhood in which there are immense areas of poverty and immense gaps in race, where there is instability and threat of instability.
We are threatened, not only with the possibility of a nuclear war but, as the hon. member who preceded me said, by the threat of environmental pollution and population explosion. These are matters that can only be dealt with effectively on an international scale; therefore, the primary object of our policy in the international field- perhaps our total policy-should be the strengthening of the UN and its member organizations. This is at least the first and the only effort that is now available to us to create the world community of which I have spoken.
There are many people responsible for diplomacy in the day-to-day conduct of foreign affairs who are, naturally, preoccupied with these day-to-day problems and sometimes have a feeling of cynicism and despair toward the United Nations. I do not blame them. There is sometimes in the UN debates a sense of futility, as has already
U.N.-Prevention of Military Aggression
been mentioned. I suggest that in the longer term point of view there is no reason for this sense of hopelessness.
There has been a forward marching of mankind toward a more effectively organized society, and there has been evidence that within this universe the spirit of creative evolution does produce the changes that are necessary. What is the Canadian contribution to this evolution? I would mention, as the hon. member for Fundy-Royal has done, the Canadian contribution to peacekeeping and to the available permanent peacekeeping forces. Canada is in a unique position to contribute in this way. We have the expertise, we are not a great power, we have the experience and we also have a degree of security from immediate aggression because of our position on the North American continent which frees us for a major effort in peacekeeping. I hope this fact will never be forgotten or disregarded because of the difficulties inevitably inherent in the development of new international institutions.
The task of the UN has only begun after 25 years. I express my gratitude to the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) who produced this motion and set these goals before us. It is easy for us to become immersed in the regional and local problems that now face us. Part of our task, however, is to look at the picture as a whole. I therefore thank the hon. member for putting these goals before us. We must not forget them.
I join the hon. member for Fundy-Royal in stressing the importance of the universality of the UN, to which reference was made by the Secretary General of the UN when he brought forward the propositions embodied in this motion and said that these things should be done now. Canada, having recognized the Peoples' Republic of China, should now urge not only the admission of China to the UN but the admission of other nations which through wars and difficulties in the past have been excluded from this world body. I hope Canada will take a clear initiative in that field.
I noticed that in the speech made by the Secretary General of the UN, U Thant, he said that to strengthen the United Nations should not be just a desire, but an obsession. I hope that many Canadians will take his words seriously and that the strength of the UN will be the centre of their policy in international affairs, one of their main purposes. That is one reason I was disappointed in the policy statement of the government respecting international affairs, namely, that it seemed to me to overlook the centrality of the development of the world community through a strengthened UN.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, this resolution has so far been supported by spokesmen for three parties-I cannot speak for the other party in the House-who have expressed their approval of the resolution which I believe embodies suggestions put forward recently by the Secretary General of the United Nations. I wonder why, instead of the resolution being talked out-which would seem to be the

November 6, 1970
U.N.-Prevention of Military Aggression usual procedure during this hour-we could not pass it. I think this would be a healthy and useful exercise and one that would show the direction in which all members of this House, regardless of party, wish our Parliament to move.

subsubtopic: UNITED NATIONS-MORE EFFECTIVE ROLE IN PREVENTING MILITARY AGGRESSION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before the House this afternoon, proposed by the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) is most fitting because it deals with the United Nations and initiatives which the government should take in reforming that body. This motion is being debated a few days after the UN completed a quarter-century of existence. With reference to the twenty-fifth anniversary of the United Nations, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said:
Over the past 25 years disillusionment and failure has not been a stranger to the UN but there has been as well substantial progress in efforts to achieve peace, justice and progress-the theme chosen by the United Nations for its anniversary year.
He also paid tribute to Canada's efforts in these words:
I am proud of the efforts that Canada and Canadians have made in support of the United Nations in the past. We have made a substantial contribution to its peace-keeping efforts, the gains that it has made in economic and social progress, its achievements in the field of human rights.
The twenty-fifth anniversary of the UN, which was celebrated on October 24, was more of a time of stocktaking than a time for celebration. The motion of the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace suggests many areas of responsibility which could well be reformed. I believe that many of these reforms are necessary and desirable. However, when we consider the problems of governing within a single nation, we realize the difficulties of bringing together a world assembly like the UN. The wonder is that it functions at all when one considers the immense complexity of national positions represented there and the diverse objectives of its members. In many ways it has been a success. Consider its membership. Now, 126 countries are members, whereas in 1945 there were only 51 countries. This is a move toward one of the objectives of the hon. member's motion, that is, universality of membership.
In its role as peacekeeper, the UN has provided a diplomatic meeting ground for conflicting nations where their disputes can be aired under the bright lights of world public opinion. This is probably the greatest value of the UN in world peacekeeping. Because of the development of instant world communication and international interdependence, every country now is concerned with its international image. The UN provides, also, a forum for other countries to use their prestige and influence on countries in conflict with one another to "cool" the situation. Usually this involves the two super powers, the U.S.A. and the U.S.S.R., using their influence on the conflicting nations. However, sometimes it works in reverse when the superpowers are in conflict. Then their positions in a dispute are held up to the scrutiny of world public opinion.
It is important to note how much emphasis the two superpowers place upon gaining world support for their actions. If this were the only value of the UN, to provide a world forum to air conflicts between nations, it would be well worth while. Consider some of the conflicts which have been handled in its 25 years' history. Nearly every one of these confrontations would have had far worse results without the influence of the United Nations.
First, the Berlin blockade was settled at an earlier stage than would have otherwise been possible. Second, the six-day war, in 1967, in the Middle East was stopped much sooner by a public airing at the UN. Third, it has hastened the transition to independence of virtually the whole of Africa south of the Sahara, and much of Asia as well. In other countries the break-up of colonial empires has resulted in far more bloodshed than in these. Only in the Congo did the transition to independence threaten to trigger great power conflict. But if there have been many successes, there has also been some decline in the authority and influence of the UN. President Nixon appointed a commission last July to propose recommendations on the course of future United States policy toward the world body. The report said that the UN is becoming increasingly incapable of dealing with issues facing the world.
The report went on to say that the failure of member nations to make the world body the paramount means for maintaining international peace and security, and its misuses into becoming an ineffective debating society and a propaganda platform, has caused the United Nations to fall short of the world's hopes. The governments of too many nations have either given lip service to the principles of the UN charter or have interpreted them for petty advantages and narrow self-interest.
The report indicated four major areas in which imaginative initiatives could revitalize the world body and make US participation more effective. First, strengthening of the UN peacekeeping machinery and improving conciliation procedures, which is particularly important in light of the Middle East situation. Second, reforming UN institutions to reduce inefficient procedures of the General Assembly, eliminate red tape, apply the rule of relevance to debate and improve the personnel selection for the secretariat. Third, developing international policies, regulations and machinery to make the United Nations capable of dealing with the worldwide effects of environmental changes brought about by accelerated scientific and technological developments. Fourth, strengthening international law and co-operation to deal with drug abuse and the hijacking of commercial airplanes, which the report described as the two current, critical problems of modern society.
Needless to say, agreement on reform of the machinery for settling international disputes will be slow and difficult, but should be pursued just the same. The right of veto by one of the permanent members of the Security Council has immobilized this body. I think this should be changed so that a single member cannot frustrate the will of the minority of representatives on the Security

November 6, 1970

Council. The overriding influence of the U.S.A. and U.S.S.R. creates a balancing-act situation in many disputes, with the free world countries lining up against the Communist world countries.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has recommended universality of membership in the United Nations. Doubtless, this would include Communist China which has 700 million people. There can be little doubt that China will eventually be seated in the United Nations. Canada has extended diplomatic recognition this year, the second country to do so in the western hemisphere. We should also support her membership in the world body. Then this government, which represents such a large percentage of the world's population, will be subject to the same responsibility as other members of the United Nations. There can be little doubt that this will further complicate the negotiation of international disputes at the United Nations. However, the Chinese influence will be direct, with the other superpowers, and will not be felt through intermediaries and through other voices outside the United Nations.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
Another area of increasing concern is the method of financing the United Nations. The Secretary General, U Thant, said recently:
The UN's financial situation is worse than ever before and steadily deteriorating. Certain governments continue to withhold contributions ... The amounts owed by slow payers continue to rise. At certain times this year the United Nations did not have enough funds to meet salary payments earned by the UN staff.
It is interesting to note in passing that the world's military budget last year came to $185 billion, foreign aid throughout the world came to $8 billion, while the budget for the UN and its agencies came to less than $200 million.
I have mentioned some of the problem areas of the UN, but there are many activities which have been notable successes, and new areas of responsibility in which I think this organization can give leadership. The hon. member's motion has outlined these. The social and economic programs of the UN have been the most successful in the past. Millions of people in underdeveloped countries have benefited from these programs. Perhaps if these programs are expanded on and developed, and the disparity between the rich and the poor nations of the world decreased, there will be fewer international disputes to be settled in the Security Council.
I am optimistic that the UN can be a positive force in influencing international control over pollution and the preservation of the environment. In 1972 a conference is to be held in Sweden to deal with this very problem. Other problems of the future, like airplane hijacking, control of development of the seabed and world population control are especially appropriate for the UN to deal with because their effects cut across national boundaries. The history of this organization leads me to believe that the UN can do a great deal in coping with these problems.
U.N.-Prevention of Military Aggression
My feelings about the future of the UN, Mr. Speaker, are similar to those in a statement made by the former Prime Minister and Member of Parliament for Algoma East, Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson, who recently said:
The United Nations has now survived 25 years of international tension and cold war. With all its faults, but also with its achievements, it remains the indispensible international institution.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is so vast a subject and we have so little time, but I of course agree that we must look toward a more effective instrument when we look upon the United Nations. The motion as set out might be realistically described as something of an overexpectation, and yet we do tend to grasp beyond our reach; and that is the inner part of wisdom down through the ages.
Speaking on the question of universality, the countries which are out are those which are divided, and their problems are not those that seem to be susceptible to United Nations resolution. Would we gain much if it should eventuate that the People's Republic of China should become a member of the United Nations, and at the same time the Nationalist Chinese be sent out into limbo? This would not be a contribution toward universality, and I hope something is being done by the Canadian government-which has been so active in working toward diplomatic recognition of Red China, something with which I do not disagree-to find a way whereby the Taiwan regime may find its place in the diplomatic community, and certainly in the United Nations. This is my comment on the question of universality.
With reference to peace forces, it is terribly important as the years go by, for instance in Cyprus, that we move away from the military or paramilitary aspect of the question and turn more to the realm of mediation and conciliation. I wonder, too, with respect to some of the organizations already activated-for example, the UNWRA meetings year after year after year, voting sums of money to the Palestine refugees but year after year after year the problem becoming more acute and painful-whether new approaches should be taken. As well as thinking of activating new areas, we must energize ourselves more in those areas which are already technically active.

Mr. Speaker, all hon. members naturally have the right to express opinions on this important notice of motion put forward but the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand).
The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) took 12 to 14 minutes to express his views. However, at the end of his speech, he said that all other members should remain silent and approve the member's resolution.
As for any initiative to be taken regarding the United Nations, it is important to remember how fragile the organization is.

U.N.-Prevention of Military Aggression
I do not share the pessimism of such as believe the United Nations headquarters to be merely a place where speeches are made. The United Nations have a role, if only that of giving politicians of the world an opportunity to meet on neutral ground. When undertaking initiatives, one should always make sure they have a chance of succeeding. If they are not welcome, they will not achieve universality, as the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) mentioned. This would undermine the very basis of the United Nations principle of universality.

If you ever send ambassadors, make sure they will be acceptable; that they will be welcome.
